For more information, contact Candace Bowers at candace.bowers@mountainview.gov Immigrant House Update By Marina Marinovich MVHA Publicity Chair At the community meeting held March 5th in the MV Senior Center, residents made a strong push for the creation of a new park at 771 North Rengstorff Avenue that preserves the existing wooded environment and includes new gardens, fixtures, benches, and lighting, and a new home for the city's historic Immigrant House. Residents in attendance were passionate about the proposed park. More than 50 people attended the meeting at the Senior Center, including representation from MVHA. Generally all agreed that the 1.2acre park should not have the parking lots and grass turf that are typical of most parks in the city. It has taken three years and the efforts of many community members to preserve Immigrant House; the 1880s structure was originally located downtown at 166 Bryant Street. Many people would like to see it become a static period-correct display of everyday life for the 1880s to 1920s immigrants. The 400-square-foot house is currently in a city storage yard and is slated to be restored and moved into the new park. The Stiepers—the park's former owners—laid out and preserved the property as a wooded oasis; every inch of it is like a precious jewel. If you were to take a bird's-eye view of the property, you would see that it is set in a sea of concrete. As Mountain View continues to grow at an accelerated pace, we need balance; we need an area to just "chill" with nature. Let's let the bees be the busiest thing on the property. Resident Deb Henigson said "Let me teach my daughter about all the trees" in the park, that is generously shaded by 164 trees, including fruit trees—apricots, figs, avocados, peaches, apples, oranges, and plums—trees that were planted in huge groves in the area's early history. The neighbors whose apartments overlook the park said they enjoy the fact that it seems to be a haven for wildlife. Someone suggested that it become a part of a Garden for Wildlife Program. One person at the meeting suggested that parking would be necessary for people interested in helping with gardening, but many others immediately disagreed, saying the park should be mostly for the neighborhood and those who choose to walk or bike there. "I don't want to add parking spaces, but it would be nice to add bicycle racks," said one man. No one argued in favor of cutting into the wooded 1.2-acre space for parking after that. Our six panelists included Helen Hughes and Karen McGough, who both grew up in the area when it was still rural; Bob Lawrence, Ken Alsman, and Kevin Duggan, three former city employees whose collective planning and leadership guided the area's growth from the 1960s to the 2010s; and Ginny Kaminkski, a longtime volunteer with Shoreline at Mountain View and the Rengstorff House. The discussion was moderated by our Newsletter Editor, Nick Perry, and covered a wide range of topics—from rural farm life, roving Hells Angels gangs, early city negotiations with developers, the transformation of the city dump into Shoreline at Mountain View, and even some ghost stories from the Rengstorff House! Our Historical Data Chair, Eugene Sharp, filmed the discussion, and we are investigating whether to air it on KMVT. We are also working on transcribing the conversation for our archives. For some memorable quotes from each of our panelists, take a look at the next page. A big THANK YOU to each of them and everyone who joined us! Hope to see you at our next event! When Shoreline Was Stierlin: Memories of the North Bayshore 5 "I had a fellow stop by [the Rengstorff House] one day and said he had lived there as a rental property with his family, and he said he had "feelings" about the house. So I said, "T ell me about your feelings!" He said "….well, things happened." He said he had a broken leg and he was upstairs in bed, and there's a door that went up to the widow's walk. There was a dresser against it, and that dresser moved, and he felt an impression at the end of his bed. Several other people have mentioned things. Our maintenance man who would come early in the mornings said he would put things in one spot or turn a light on and go outside to do something, and things had changed. So, I would be working there [alone] late at night and I'd say "If anybody wants to tell me anything, I'll listen to ya!" –Ginny Kaminski, former Program Coordinator, Shoreline at Mountain View "One story that I remember that really emphasizes the changes that have been made—my street, Plymouth Street, went across Bayshore. It wasn't called 101, it was Bayshore. With a stop sign! And the little store on our side didn't carry magazines, but the one on the other side did, and we used to walk across Bayshore to buy our magazines and walk back home. So, quite a change!" –Karen Howard McGough, grew up in one of the last houses still standing in the North Bayshore "I lived on Stierlin Road right where the amphitheater is—so I have all the celebrities in my backyard! I was from a family of five people. My mother and father had a nice farm with an acre and a half. We had every fruit tree, every animal, all on that acre and a half. It was a very nice life, a small community of small farmers so to see it become one of the richest areas in the world is purely amazing to me." –Helen Hughes, grew up on a farm on the site of Shoreline Amphitheatre "...they [Bob Lawrence and Ken Alsman] decided to pay me $3 an hour to go out on foot and walk through the entire area and survey what was actually out there. The main thing I remember was being chased by every junkyard dog. There were some wonderful people out there, really interesting land uses, a real variety of things, and some real mean dogs!" –Kevin Duggan, Mountain View City Manager, 1990–2011 and Planning Intern, 1971–1972 "Just before the war, the freeway had been built, 101. As I recall, it seemed like that area was kind of divorced from the rest of the town. I remember when I first came here in the 1960s I thought, "Gee, this is a town with a waterfront, but not many people were even aware that there was a water frontage to our community." –Robert (Bob) Lawrence, Mountain View Planning Director, 1962–1975 "The North Bayshore was the Wild West. It really was. I know people living there saw it as kind of being a really wonderful place. But for this guy from New Jersey, it was the Wild West. The roads were kind of funky. There were Hells Angels living in a couple of the houses out there. Y ou could always find some sort of a cock fight or something going on in the neighborhood. And I distinctly remember a guy living in a teepee! I don't know why." –Ken Alsman, Mountain View City Planner, 1968–1995 Memorable Quotes Winter 2014 Event Recap Cont. 6 Eunice & Sleeper AVE 100 Street T alk By Candace Bowers MVHA Vice President In anticipation of our Spring event at 655 Eunice Avenue, let's take a look back at the history of the street and its neighbor to the north, Sleeper Avenue. If you live on Eunice Avenue today, you might not be able to tell from your cheerful, modern surroundings that your street has a link to Mountain View's earliest settlers—and an "otherwordly" connection, too. Eunice Avenue was named for Eunice Sleeper, who was married to one of Mountain View's early pioneers, Frank Sleeper. A prominent citizen in her own right, Eunice was also an ardent spiritualist. Eunice was born 1813 in Maine, and came to California in 1850 with her husband. They settled in Mountain View in 1852. Their land was bordered by present-day El Camino Real, Phyllis Avenue, and Stevens Creek, and included the land that later became the Dale Ranch. Frank served as a school trustee and member of the County Board of Supervisors. After he died in 1872, Eunice—having no surviving children—created the Sleeper Trust, funded by the sale of her considerable land holdings and dedicated to her and her husband's shared cause: spiritualism. 1876 map showing "Mrs. E.S. Sleeper Ranch" 1938 map showing Eunice and Sleeper Ave. Maps from the David Rumsey map collection: www.davidrusmey.org April 30, 1915 San Jose Evening News Article At the time, spiritualism—the belief that the dead can communicate with the living (and are encouraged to do so)—was quite popular, if not mainstream. The Trust was able to support spiritualist endeavors as well as pay Eunice's living expenses at the Pratt Home for Old Ladies in San Jose. In 1899, the Trust bought the former YMCA building in downtown San Jose; renamed as Sleeper Hall, it became the headquarters for the First Spiritual Union of San Jose. It also hosted meetings of other local groups, and was the site of Eunice's own funeral in 1901. Sleeper Hall later became the San Jose Labor Temple, of which Jack London is said to have been a member. The building was torn down in the 1950s. 7 The Mountain View Historical Association welcomes new members! Meet the New MVHA Board Members! As we begin 2015, the MVHA is very excited to welcome three new faces to our Board of Directors! Learn a bit about each of them here. Candace Bowers MVHA Vice President Candace Bowers has worked at the Mountain View Public Library for 24 years, at the adult reference desk and more recently in the Mountain View History Center. She is a Bay Area native and a 2008 graduate of Leadership Mountain View. She enjoys taking students on tours of the History Center, and leading craft workshops for adults. Mary Kay "Marina" Marinovich MVHA Publicity Chair Mary Kay "Marina" Marinovich is a Mountain View native who grew up on an apricot/ cherry orchard at Grant Road and Oak Avenue. She is the daughter of a Croatian immigrant and lived in a time when apricots were once more plentiful than silicon chips. She is a lead advocate for the saving of Immigrant House (see article on Page 4); a project she hopes will become a historic display in the new park at 771 N. Rengstorff Avenue and will be a tribute to Mountain View's agrarian past and immigrant laborers. She currently serves on the Board of the Mountain View Kiwanis Club and is Old Mountain View Neighborhood Association Historic Sub Committee Chair. Preserving our history, our native wildlife and our heritage tree canopy are causes that are dear to her heart. Lisa Roquero Garcia MVHA Director-at-Large Lisa Roquero Garcia is a life-long resident of Mountain View. She is part of the thirdgeneration of her family to call the city home. Her mother's side has deep roots in the city's Mexican American community, her father's side in the city's Filipino American community. She is excited to join the MVHA Board and help share Mountain View's rich and diverse history with the community. 4 By Mary Kay "Marina" Marinovich Publicity Chair Editors Note: Marina Marinovich is leading efforts to restore the "Immigrant House" which stood behind the historic Pearson House at 902 Villa Street (dem. in 2013). Here, Marina offers an update on the future of the Immigrant House. It's official! Immigrant House is to be incorporated into the design of Mountain View's newest park. The Old Mountain View neighborhood's 1880s historic little laborer's house has been saved and will be included in the design of the 1.22 acre park at 771 North Rengstorff Ave. On December 9, the City Council approved a staff recommendation for Callander and Associates Inc. to provide design services for the park in the amount not to exceed $168,100. This group has worked with several cities on very successful park projects, which include moving the Neutra House in Los Altos, and designing both the Stojanovich Family Park in Campbell as well as the J. Neely Johnson Community Garden in Sacramento. Once Immigrant House has been renovated and relocated to the new park, it will stand as a humble remnant of Old Mountain View's pioneer past. It is to be hoped that the property will remain as undisturbed and natural as possible as it is a jewel of a site, reminding Mountain View residents of the city's agrarian roots. The park will also provide indigenous wildlife a sanctuary, something hard to come by in the very busy North Rengstorff area. Important Marina Marinovich (left) and Francis Stieper (right) on the Stieper family property - future park and home of the Immigrant House. as well, is that the preserved little house itself will be educational for future generations. Structurally, Immigrant House incorporates building techniques that have not been seen in more than 100 years. It also exemplifies the difficult living conditions that immigrants endured while trying to improve their lives in America. It is probably the oldest surviving home in Mountain View, and the last remaining laborer's cottage in Santa Clara Valley. That it lasted in the downtown Mountain View neighborhood until 2012 is a miracle unto itself! Its tenants and those of others like it built the infrastructure that made Mountain View what it is today. Prospective donors are expressing interest in the use of the structure, which will be determined during the design of the park. The Friends of Immigrant House hope to exhibit the house as a static display. To this end, they have been given a nine month extension to raise funds equaling $113,500. $55,000 has been raised so far. Appealing to donors to raise the remaining $58,500 will be easier now that a design plan offering specifics is on its way, thanks to the City Council's staff recommendation approval. The other structure which is currently located on the park is the original Stieper home, built in the 1950s by the Stiepers themselves. Building one's own home was very common during that era. Historically, the home is a part of the property's story. It dates back just prior to the suburbanization that replaced all the orchards and dairies of the area. Modern historians now say there is an alarming tendency to destroy structures built in the 50s and 60s, much the way many Victorians were torn down during the 20s and 30s. If a supported use for the structure can be found, there is the possibility it will not be destroyed. So what are your thoughts? Keep the original home built by the Stiepers and turn it to a garden gift shop like the Allied Arts Guild of Menlo Park, a museum, a meeting area for clubs, a place for knitting groups and arts and crafts enthusiasts to gather? Or how about a new Mountain View Gardening Club, or maybe even a history museum? Conversely, because of its close proximity to the road, the home could be demolished in order to create an area for busses to pull into in order to facilitate visits to the park by school children. This is everyone's new park, so please give the city your input; they are open to your ideas and want to listen. Immigrant House Update STIEPER FAMILY PROPERTY 4 Want to learn more? The aims of the MVHA are: • To gather and preserve historical data relative to the early settlement and development of the area in and around the present City of Mountain View. • To collect, record, edit and publish a history of the pioneering activities of this area • To preserve historic objects and places • To cooperate with other organizations in the Santa Clara Valley on projects deemed worthy by our membership Membership Report By June Casey Membership Chair Membership as of December 19, 2014 Honored Members 2 Life Members 115 Family Members 78 Single Members 115 TOTAL MEMBERSHIP 311 New Life Member: Lucas Ramirez New Members: David T .
